scenarios.title: Pressure behind the receiver
scenarios.objective: Prepare for a pass while checking pressure outside the receiver’s forward view.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 holds the puck and is preparing a pass toward YOU. YOU face F1; D1 waits behind your up-ice shoulder. F2 offers a different direction after reception.
cues: F1 has not released the puck.
YOU face the passer.
D1 is behind YOU relative to that facing.

questions.prompt: Who still owns the puck before the proposed pass?

options.text: F1
YOU
D1

questions.explanation: F1 is the designated carrier; YOU are preparing to receive.

questions.prompt: Which information matters before YOU turn up ice?

options.text: Whether D1 is closing
Whether F2 remains available
Whether the pass has actually reached your stick

questions.explanation: All three affect a turn or next pass. An intended reception must not be treated as completed possession.

questions.prompt: Order this receiving-and-next-read suggestion.

options.text: Check the space behind you
Receive the pass under control
Choose the next action using the updated space

questions.explanation: This routine separates preparation, possession and decision; another scan during reception may be useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a receiving spot that separates you from D1.
questions.explanation: The example opens a diagonal from F1 and more separation from D1. It is one option, not a required skating route.

questions.prompt: If D1 stays far back and the lane ahead remains open after reception, what becomes an option?

options.text: A controlled carry into that space
An automatic pass back every time
Turn up ice before confirming the pass arrived

questions.explanation: An open lane can support carrying. F2 or a return pass may still be useful if their evidence is better.

questions.prompt: Why is facing the passer not enough information for this reception?
questions.explanation: A receiver can see the puck while missing pressure from another direction. Explain what you would check and how it affects your next touch.

questions.prompt: What should YOU learn before F1 releases the pass?

options.text: Where D1 is and whether the wider shoulder is reachable
Which turn is mandatory
That F2 will receive next

questions.explanation: The pressure location and the reachable receiving shoulder explain why the reception can stay adaptable.

questions.prompt: Which two signs support receiving away from D1?

options.text: F1 can see the wider target
D1 remains inside rather than closing the target
F2 is up ice even if the pass lane is covered

questions.explanation: The passer's view and D1's position make the target useful; F2 is a later read.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a shoulder that opens F1's lane and leaves D1 inside.
questions.explanation: The changed angle separates YOU from D1 while preserving a route from F1.

questions.prompt: D1 reaches your inside shoulder as the puck arrives. Explain the changed reception and next scan.
questions.explanation: Protect the first touch away from D1, then scan whether F2 or a return lane remains. A turn is conditional on the space that is still there.

scenarios.title: Step out of the shaded lane
scenarios.objective: Recognize that a teammate can be nearby yet unavailable on a direct passing line.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 has possession. YOU are a nearby receiver, but D1 stands between you and the puck. F2 is farther across the ice. The task is to improve your own availability.
cues: D1 occupies the direct F1-to-YOU line.
F2 offers a separate angle.
Being nearest is different from having a clear lane.

questions.prompt: Which player stands on the direct line between F1 and YOU?

options.text: F2
D1
No player

questions.explanation: D1 sits between the carrier and your current receiving spot.

questions.prompt: What could make your support more useful?

options.text: Create a different angle from F1
Keep track of D1 as you move
Stand closer even if D1 stays in the same line

questions.explanation: Changing the angle can expose a lane. Closing distance alone does not remove the obstruction.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple re-offer routine.

options.text: Notice the blocked line
Move into a different passing angle
Check whether F1 can still see and reach you

questions.explanation: This is a suggested way to solve this obstruction; the carrier may choose another action meanwhile.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away from D1’s current passing shadow.
questions.explanation: The sample shifts across the line instead of only closer to F1. Other separated angles may work.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 follows your new route. What is a useful next read?

options.text: Assume the lane must still be open
Stay in the new spot without checking F1
Look for another angle or space opened for F2

questions.explanation: A defender’s response changes which lane is useful. Your movement can also help a teammate.

questions.prompt: How would you tell the difference between “closer” and “more available” here?
questions.explanation: Describe the carrier-to-receiver line and the defender in it, rather than relying only on distance.

questions.prompt: What is the useful communication after D1 blocks the first line?

options.text: I will re-offer above the line; check whether you can reach me
The first lane is open even if the picture changes
F2 must stay wide and never move

questions.explanation: The message names the changed angle and keeps F1's pass conditional on reachability.

questions.prompt: Which two responses could follow D1's reaction to your re-offer?

options.text: Use the new lane if F1 can reach it
Notice space D1 leaves for F2 if D1 follows
Hold the same direct lane while D1 remains between F1 and YOU

questions.explanation: D1's response creates the next decision: use the lane, or exploit the space that the defender left.

questions.prompt: Move YOU across the blocked line into a visible support angle.
questions.explanation: This point changes the F1-to-YOU line and keeps F2 separate.

questions.prompt: F1 carries while D1 follows you. Explain the value of your movement.
questions.explanation: Your movement can pull D1 and open F2 or F1's carry lane. Call the open space, then re-check it because D1 may recover.

scenarios.title: A new job after your pass
scenarios.objective: Plan off-puck movement after a completed pass without assuming an immediate return.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU have just passed to F2, who now owns the puck. D1 lies between your old position and F2. This freeze begins after reception, not during flight.
cues: F2 owns the puck now.
YOU no longer need to carry it.
D1 shades the old return line.

questions.prompt: What changed when the stated pass finished?

options.text: YOU kept possession through the completed pass
F2 became the puck carrier
Both YOU and F2 now own the puck

questions.explanation: The briefing and ownership both identify F2 as the receiver in possession.

questions.prompt: Which choices keep YOU involved without owning the puck?

options.text: Offer a fresh return angle
Notice where D1 follows
Remain in the old return line without checking D1

questions.explanation: Off-puck support means remaining useful as the carrier and defence change.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested continuation after reception.

options.text: Recognize that F2 now has possession
Find space outside the old return line
Show a new option and read D1 again

questions.explanation: The routine begins from actual reception. It does not promise a second pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to offer a new return angle for F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves beyond the old obstruction. A shorter lateral option can also work if it creates a usable line.

questions.prompt: If F2 carries forward instead of returning the puck, what could YOU do?

options.text: Adjust support to F2’s new location
Insist that F2 pass back immediately
Stay at the original pass location without another look

questions.explanation: Support follows the actual carrier. The initial pass does not require a scripted return.

questions.prompt: What might your movement accomplish even if F2 never passes back?
questions.explanation: It could offer support, move a defender or leave another lane available. Identify which relationship you expect to change.

questions.prompt: After F2 receives, what should YOU communicate?

options.text: I am changing the support angle; tell me if the return lane opens
The puck must come straight back
My first pass is complete because I passed

questions.explanation: The message matches the new carrier and keeps the return conditional while support continues.

questions.prompt: Which two details decide where to support F2?

options.text: F2's direction with the puck
D1's coverage of the old return line
The fact that YOU passed once

questions.explanation: The current carrier and defender coverage describe the new job; the earlier pass does not fix the next spot.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a support point outside the direct return lane between your old position and F2.
questions.explanation: This point gives F2 a different support relationship outside the direct return lane while keeping D1 visible; the lane is inferred from the named players.

questions.prompt: F2 carries toward the middle and D1 turns with F2. What do you do next?
questions.explanation: Match support to F2’s new position, keep D1’s route in view, and communicate whether YOU can stay available for a return pass if F2 needs it.

scenarios.title: An outlet behind half-wall pressure
scenarios.objective: Notice when a supporting player behind the carrier can offer a reset.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 owns the puck near the half wall, the side-board area partway into the attacking zone, and D1 is ahead of the carrier. YOU are also ahead of F1 but nearer the middle. Consider offering an option away from the forward pressure.
cues: The immediate pressure is ahead of F1.
YOU currently stand up ice of F1.
Space behind F1 is not occupied by a shown defender.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes YOU’s starting position?

options.text: Behind F1 toward the left end
Ahead of F1 toward the right end
Level with F1 toward the same goal line

questions.explanation: YOU have a larger x position than F1 while navy attacks +x.

questions.prompt: What should a reset outlet try to provide?

options.text: A line F1 can use
Separation from the pressuring defender
The closest possible position to the boards in every case

questions.explanation: A usable line and room matter; the still frame cannot guarantee future recovery times.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested support adjustment.

options.text: Notice the forward pressure
Offer a visible option behind it
Reassess after F1 chooses pass or carry

questions.explanation: Offering a reset adds an option without choosing F1’s action for them.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an outlet behind F1 with space from D1.
questions.explanation: The sample provides a diagonal back toward the middle. Other positions behind pressure may remain useful.

questions.prompt: Suppose D2 now moves into your reset lane. What would you reconsider?

options.text: Whether another angle or a protected hold is available
Whether the first reset must happen anyway
Whether the reset lane matters only before YOU move

questions.explanation: Recheck the new lane. A reset is useful only while the evidence supports it.

questions.prompt: What would make a backward pass helpful rather than just giving up ground?
questions.explanation: Explain what pressure it avoids and what options the new carrier might gain. Distance from the goal alone does not settle the decision.

questions.prompt: Why offer space behind F1 in this picture?

options.text: It can give F1 a reachable reset if pressure removes the forward lane
It gives F1 a reset even if D2 has taken that lane
It pulls YOU into D1's route

questions.explanation: The behind-pressure space is useful because F1 can choose it when reachable; the carrier may still carry or use another lane.

questions.prompt: Which two updates could cancel the reset?

options.text: D2 moves into the offered lane
F1 loses sight of YOU
D1 remains at the same spot

questions.explanation: D2 coverage or a lost sightline removes the reason for the reset; the unchanged D1 position alone does not decide it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU behind F1 with separation from both defenders.
questions.explanation: This reference places YOU behind F1 and away from D1, with D2 still visible for the next scan.

questions.prompt: D2 closes the reset while F1 still has the puck. Explain the next read.
questions.explanation: Name the closed reset, scan F1's remaining space and support, and choose carry, protection, or another outlet only if that lane remains usable.

scenarios.title: Find the loose rebound first
scenarios.objective: Separate a loose puck from a promised rebound goal.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The coach states that F1’s previous shot came loose to the goalie’s side. YOU are arriving away from the puck. No goal or next touch is assumed.
cues: The loose puck is on the positive-y side of the goal area.
D1 stands closer to the middle.
YOU must locate the puck before planning a second action.

questions.prompt: Where is the puck relative to the goalie at this freeze?

options.text: At centre ice
Off to one side of the goalie, still loose
Already in the goalie’s glove

questions.explanation: The puck is beside the goalie’s current area and has no owner. It is neither at centre ice nor held by the goalie.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter for your next approach?

options.text: Where the loose puck actually is
Where D1 is relative to the approach
The assumption that the next touch must be a shot

questions.explanation: Locate both puck and obstruction. A second chance still needs a real recovery and shooting opportunity.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested rebound-read routine.

options.text: Locate the loose puck
Check the approach and establish control if possible
Reassess a shot or pass

questions.explanation: This example emphasizes control and a new read. An immediate touch could be appropriate if the actual arrival supports it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to show an approach toward the loose-puck side.
questions.explanation: The example approaches from outside D1’s current middle position. It is not proof that YOU arrive first.

questions.prompt: If the goalie covers the puck before YOU arrive, what changes?

options.text: The puck is still available for a rebound shot
YOU can assume a goal
The previous loose-puck plan no longer applies

questions.explanation: A covered puck is a different state. Do not continue acting on the earlier loose-puck assumption.

questions.prompt: What extra information would you need before predicting a second shot?
questions.explanation: You might need puck movement, defender speed, control and whether play is still active. A static loose puck does not establish them.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while approaching the rebound?

options.text: Puck below the circle; D1 is between it and the net
The second shot is ours
F1 must shoot next

questions.explanation: The call names the actual puck and defender, which helps F1 understand the recovery read.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would alter the rebound plan?

options.text: D1 controls the puck
F1 becomes a reachable support option
The net stays at the same end

questions.explanation: Possession and support change the next job; the net location alone does not decide the play.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the loose puck from the opposite-side boards while keeping D1 and Gold's net in view.
questions.explanation: This point gives YOU a different side-board approach to the loose puck while preserving D1 and Gold's net in view; it does not prove arrival order or control.

questions.prompt: The goalie covers before you arrive. What do you re-read?
questions.explanation: The loose-puck option is gone, so identify who has the puck and where F1 can support before choosing the next pressure or reset.

scenarios.title: Receive into an open shoulder
scenarios.objective: Plan a receiving destination while separating a future pass from current possession.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 is preparing a pass across the neutral zone to YOU. D1 waits up ice on your middle-side shoulder. The pass has not left F1’s stick.
cues: F1 owns the puck.
D1 is beyond the receiver toward the attacking end.
Space is available farther toward the negative-y wall.

options.text: F1
D1
Both F1 and D1

options.text: A usable line from F1
Room for the next action after the touch
Only which spot is closest to the right net

questions.prompt: Order this suggested reception routine.

options.text: Offer a target in available space
Control the incoming puck
Read D1 before the next pass or carry

questions.explanation: This teaching order separates receiving from the next action; a skilled one-touch play would require different timing evidence.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a receiving point with room away from D1.
questions.explanation: The sample moves toward the side boards away from D1 while retaining a diagonal pass from F1. It is not the only receiving point.

questions.prompt: If the pass reaches behind YOU instead of the intended spot, what should the plan account for?

options.text: The actual puck location before the next action
Only the original target point
An automatic shot before possession

questions.explanation: A misplaced pass changes the task. Regain control or adjust before assuming the planned continuation.

questions.prompt: What could make receiving slightly wider useful in this picture?
questions.explanation: Connect the receiving line, D1’s position and the next available action. Wider is not always better if it closes another option.

questions.prompt: What should F1 know about your receiving target?

options.text: The wider target is available only while D1 stays inside it
I will turn up ice before locating the arriving puck
Keep aiming at my old spot if I move wider

questions.explanation: The message ties the target to D1 and F1's route, keeping the choice conditional.

questions.prompt: Which two details support the wider reception?

options.text: F1 can reach the diagonal target
D1 is not closing it yet
YOU have already chosen the next touch before checking the arrival

questions.explanation: The passer and defender cues make the target usable; the next touch still needs a scan.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a wider receiving point on the neutral-zone side of D1.
questions.explanation: The point is on the neutral-zone side of D1 and opens F1's diagonal lane; the receiving choice still depends on the actual pressure.

questions.prompt: The puck arrives behind YOU. What do you say and do?
questions.explanation: Call the miss, recover the actual puck under control, and name whether D1 or F1 changes the next option.

cues: D1 blocks the straight F1-to-YOU line.
The side boards offer a different possible route.
D2 remains nearer the middle and goal.

options.text: D2 is the current puck carrier
D1 is between F1 and YOU
YOU are the puck carrier

options.text: Where the puck might leave the boards
Whether YOU can reach its exit path
Whether the puck is guaranteed to bounce as planned

options.text: Notice the blocked direct line
Agree on a possible board route and receiving area
Read the actual rebound before the next touch

questions.explanation: The sample is closer to a board-pass exit and outside D1’s current position. Other angles may be better with real puck speed.

options.text: Whether that wall route remains open
Only how the direct route looked before D1 moved
A rule that every blocked pass must use the wall

questions.prompt: How is using the half wall different from simply passing through D1?
questions.explanation: Describe the changed puck path and the new receiving information it requires. Do not assume a successful bounce.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before the wall option?

options.text: D1 blocks the direct lane; watch the rebound near the wall
Aim at the same board spot even if I move
Use the direct pass before checking D1’s stick

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape the bank point?

options.text: Where YOU can receive the rebound
Whether D2 remains available at the opposite point
That D2 does not move

questions.prompt: Move YOU farther along the wall beyond D1.

questions.prompt: D1 turns to the wall before the pass. Explain what you recheck.

The loose puck is wider than YOU.
The original receiving spot is no longer the puck location.

Where can YOU provide an option without crowding F1’s route?
Does standing in the low slot guarantee a goal?

options.text: Notice your position in F1’s line
Choose a useful nearby role or receiving angle
Recheck as F1 changes the puck position

options.text: The new receiving line and D1’s reach
Only whether YOU are nearest the crease
The old shooting line without the puck’s new plan

questions.prompt: How could you explain “beside the shot lane” without saying “move to my dot”?
questions.explanation: Describe your relationship to F1, the goal and D1. Another point can satisfy the same relationship.

options.text: I am beside the lane; show me if the pass opens
I will occupy the same lane
The goalie guarantees a rebound

options.text: F1 changes from shot to pass
D1 follows toward your side
The goalie remains in the crease

F2 is a separate wide option.

Behind the right net

questions.prompt: After the stated missed reach, which attacker has moved beyond YOU toward the right net?

options.text: F2 has the puck behind YOU.
F1 has the puck closer to the right goal line.
YOU still own the puck.

options.text: F1’s route toward the net
F2’s possible receiving lane
Only where F1 stood before your missed reach

options.text: Recognize that the first challenge is over.
Turn and move toward a useful defensive route.
Recheck the puck and the second attacker as you recover.

questions.explanation: This is a recovery routine, not a promise that the defender can regain position. The recheck can happen repeatedly while moving.

questions.prompt: Suppose F1 then slows and turns toward the side boards while F2 drives the middle. What should update your read?

options.text: Keep reaching toward F1’s old position.
Ignore F2 because F1 owns the puck.
Recheck the middle threat and whether a teammate can handle the carrier.

questions.explanation: The developing middle route may matter more than another distant reach. Team support and actual timing determine whether YOU recover toward F2 or can challenge F1 again.

questions.prompt: Why is a second reach from behind sometimes less useful than recovering toward the net?
questions.explanation: A reach that cannot affect the puck can delay recovery and leave the middle open. Explain the distance, skating direction and second attacker; a safe reachable stick play can still be useful.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call after the missed reach?

options.text: F1 is ahead; I am recovering toward the net-side lane
The puck is won already
F2 is no longer relevant

questions.explanation: The call identifies the missed reach and the new net-side priority.

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape your recovery?

options.text: F1's route to the right net
F2's wide position
The first reach must be repeated

questions.explanation: The two attackers define the recovery relationship; repeating the reach is not a decision rule.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to the net-side space between F1 and the goal.
questions.explanation: This point recovers toward the dangerous lane while keeping F2 in view.

questions.prompt: F1 slows at the boards while F2 drives middle. Explain the updated job.
questions.explanation: Protect the new middle threat while staying connected to F1. Name which attacker is more dangerous from the changed space.

Navy F2 is moving through the other side of the middle; this movement is stated rather than animated.

F2 is a separate navy runner.
YOU defend the right net.

Whether D1 still has pressure on F1
Whether YOU can see both the runner and puck

options.text: Identify who is pressuring the carrier.
Find the separate runner and choose an inside recovery route.

questions.prompt: If D1 falls behind F1 and calls for help, how should YOU respond?

options.text: Keep the original assignment without looking again.
Recheck the immediate net threat and communicate who can cover F2.
Automatically skate to the far corner.

questions.explanation: New pressure information can change the responsibilities. Helping on the carrier may be needed, but F2’s route should remain part of the decision rather than disappearing from the read.

questions.prompt: What would make your backcheck different from simply skating toward the puck?
questions.explanation: Describe the teammate already applying pressure, the uncovered runner, and your route toward the defended net. A strong explanation also states what new cue would make you switch responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate on the backcheck?

options.text: D1 has F1; I am tracking F2 toward the right net
I am chasing the puck only
F2 does not receive

questions.prompt: Which two events can change your backcheck?

options.text: F2 cuts toward the net
D1 loses contact with F1
The puck stays with F1

questions.explanation: The runner route and teammate pressure determine whether the backcheck job shifts.

questions.prompt: Move YOU between F2 and the right net.
questions.explanation: This point places YOU on the defended net-side of F2 and keeps F1 visible; the recovery route remains conditional on F2’s movement.

questions.prompt: D1 calls for help after falling behind F1. How do you choose?
questions.explanation: Re-scan F1 and F2, then support the more dangerous reachable lane without losing sight of the second attacker.

scenarios.title: Find a job after the faceoff breaks loose

The coach assigns navy C to contest it against gold C. YOU are navy and look for a useful next-pass option. These are after-faceoff positions, not legal starting positions.

The faceoff has already happened.
Navy C has the first loose-puck assignment.

Gold F2’s position near the support side
Only which team YOU expect to win the faceoff

Find a visible support lane away from the same contest.
React to the team that actually wins control.

options.text: Turn the support read into a defensive recovery read.
Keep asking for the pass expected from a navy faceoff win
Keep treating the puck as a guaranteed navy win.

questions.explanation: The losing team’s next job depends on the new carrier and outlets. YOU should identify the immediate threat and recover with teammates rather than continue a pass request based on the expected winner.

questions.prompt: Why does “after the faceoff” still require a possession check?
questions.explanation: A faceoff can produce a loose puck or a second contest. The drop itself does not tell you which team controls the next play; support and recovery should follow the actual outcome.

options.text: I am above the play; tell me who controls before I support
Navy owns it already
Gold must win it

questions.prompt: Which two updates determine your second-play route?

options.text: The centre who gains control
F2's position after the contest
The faceoff label itself

questions.explanation: Wait for the carrier cue, then name whether you support Navy or recover against Gold. The faceoff label alone does not set your job.

scenarios.title: Support the corner retriever from the slot side
scenarios.objective: Separate retrieval and support jobs around a loose puck in the corner.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The puck is loose in the right-end corner. The coach names navy F2 as the retriever for this rep. YOU are navy and can offer support toward the slot, the central space in front of the net. Gold D1 is between the corner area and the net.

F2 has the retrieval assignment.
D1 is between that corner and the net.

questions.prompt: Which fact gives YOU a different first job from navy F2?

options.text: YOU have a different jersey colour.
The coach has assigned F2 to retrieve the loose corner puck.
Gold D1 has already passed to YOU.

questions.prompt: Which checks help YOU choose slot-side support instead of following F2 into the same corner?

options.text: The potential route from F2 to YOU after control
D1’s position between the corner and net
Enough separation for F2 to handle the puck

questions.explanation: Support is useful when it gives the retriever an option and avoids crowding the same space. The defender may still close the pass, so a slot-side spot must be read rather than assumed open.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested response to the assigned corner retrieval.

options.text: Recognize F2’s retrieval job.
Find a separated support position and check D1.

questions.explanation: The reference moves away from the corner contest and toward the central side while staying farther out than the net-front defender. Other support heights can work; D1 and the eventual puck position determine whether a pass is available.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 reaches the puck first and carries out of the corner. What changes for YOU?

options.text: Keep waiting for the assigned F2 pass.
Assume F2 still owns it because F2 was the retriever.
Read the gold possession and help pressure or recover with F2.

questions.explanation: An assigned task does not guarantee the outcome. A gold regain changes the play, so YOU should respond to the actual carrier and teammates rather than the planned retrieval.

questions.prompt: How can YOU help a corner retrieval without being the closest navy player to the puck?
questions.explanation: A separated receiving option can help F2 move the puck away from pressure after gaining control. Explain where the slot-side option is, how D1 affects the route, and what YOU would change if the puck stays loose or gold wins it.

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell F2 from above the corner?

options.text: I am above you; use me if the slot-side lane stays open
I will enter the same corner
The exit is certain

questions.explanation: The message offers slot-side support and keeps it conditional on the exit lane.

questions.prompt: Which two details shape the support angle?

options.text: F2's ability to see YOU
D1's route after the pickup
The loose puck guarantees a pass

questions.explanation: The carrier view and defender response determine whether the support angle remains useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a slot-side point between F2 and Gold's net.
questions.explanation: This point supports from the slot side between F2 and Gold's net while leaving F2 room to work; it does not decide who reaches the loose puck first.

questions.prompt: D1 wins the puck and exits. What changes for YOU?
questions.explanation: Switch to a defensive relationship with D1 or the next runner, using the left-right direction and visible support to choose.

scenarios.title: Reset behind the blue line in a timing drill

F1 waits with the puck. This is a practice reset condition, not a complete offside lesson or an officiating ruling.

The right blue line separates the neutral zone from the attacking end.
F1 is waiting with the puck on the neutral-zone side.

questions.prompt: F2 carries toward the middle instead of returning. What should YOU do?

options.text: Adjust support relative to F2 and call the available lane
Follow F2’s route without checking D1’s new lane
Hold the old return point without checking F2’s route

questions.explanation: Support follows the actual carrier. Update F2’s route and D1’s lane instead of chasing blindly or holding the old return point.

questions.prompt: What can your support accomplish when F2 keeps the puck?
questions.explanation: It can pull D1, offer a second lane, or protect F2's next option. Describe the named space and make the benefit conditional on D1's response.

scenarios.title: Protect on the outside shoulder
scenarios.objective: Use your body position to keep a carrier option while pressure closes from inside.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. YOU carries near the right-side lane with D1 inside and F2 higher in the middle. The practice constraint is one controlled touch before choosing to protect, carry, or use F2.
cues: YOU carries near the right-side lane.
D1 approaches from inside.
F2 is a higher middle option.

options.text: Keeping D1 on the inside shoulder
Knowing whether F2 remains reachable
Turning away from every teammate

questions.explanation: The body-side relationship and F2's availability explain why protection can preserve choices; the next touch depends on the updated lane.

questions.prompt: Arrange a pressure-protection read.

options.text: Locate D1 and F2
Use one controlled touch away from pressure
Choose carry, hold or pass after the touch

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a holding point farther outside while keeping F2 in view.
questions.explanation: This point shifts toward the outside edge and away from D1, while F2 remains visible.

questions.prompt: D1 follows outside and F2 opens inside. What becomes worth checking?

options.text: Whether F2 can now receive from your protected position
Keep the outside carry after D1 follows, ignoring F2’s new inside lane
Leave F2’s new lane unused and keep the puck on the wall

questions.explanation: D1’s movement changes the inside lane. Check whether F2 can receive from the protected position before choosing a carry or pass.

questions.prompt: How can protecting the puck help F2 without forcing a pass?
questions.explanation: Keeping D1 on one side can buy time for F2 to become visible or draw coverage. The pass remains conditional on F2's lane and pressure.

cues: Open space is ahead of YOU.
D1 is ahead and inside.
F2 is wide ahead, but the lane can change.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should change a carry decision?

options.text: Whether the forward lane stays open
Whether D1 can close from inside
That F2 is wide so the carry must continue

questions.explanation: The lane and defender movement explain whether carrying preserves space; F2 is an option, not a command.

questions.prompt: Arrange the open-space scan.

options.text: Check the lane and D1
Take the controlled touch
Re-read F2 and the next lane

questions.prompt: D1 turns and reaches the wide lane before your next touch. What should you change?

options.text: Protect or use F2 if that lane remains reachable
Continue wide because the first lane was open
Stop and wait for D1 to choose

questions.explanation: D1 has changed the lane. Check whether protection or F2 now gives a safer continuation.

questions.prompt: What movement from D1 would make you stop carrying forward?
questions.explanation: A turn that closes the lane ahead or cuts off your support should trigger a re-read. Explain where F2 or a protected touch could replace the carry.

YOU is inside F1.
F2 trails on the far side.

A chance to chase F2 wide immediately
A predictable carrier path regardless of movement

Match the inside relationship
Update if F1 cuts back

questions.prompt: F1 cuts back toward centre ice. What should you reassess?

options.text: Your inside relationship and the space F1 now wants
Continue toward the wall as if F1 stayed wide
Follow F2 instead of the carrier

questions.explanation: The cut-back changes F1's route and the inside gap. Re-match the carrier while protecting the middle.

questions.prompt: How would you describe this angle using the slot and half wall?
